Virtually all known algorithms for parameter estimation in Gaussian Mixture Models (GMMs)—from the foundational work of [ pearson1894contributions ] to recent advances in theoretical computer science ( e.g. , [ hopkins2018mixture , kothari2018robust , liu2022clustering ] )—are fundamentally moment-based . A spectacular use of the method of moments was the sequence of classical works that settled the efficient learnability of a high-dimensional mixture of Gaussians [ kalai2010efficiently , moitra2010settling , belkin2010polynomial , hardt2015tight ] under minimal information-theoretic separation assumptions. Subsequent work, including [ hsu2013learning , bhaskara2014uniqueness , anderson2014more , ge2015learning , bhaskara2014smoothed ] , leveraged tensor decomposition techniques, focusing on extracting low-rank structure from empirical third- and fourth-order moment tensors—structures that are especially tractable in the case of Gaussian mixtures. Motivated by applications to robust statistics, recent works [ hopkins2018mixture , kothari2018robust , diakonikolas2018list ] introduced the use of higher moments to enable parameter estimation with separation as small as k ε k^{\varepsilon} for any ε > 0 \varepsilon>0 , even beyond the Gaussian setting.
